text: Affect labelling: naming a feeling in plain words tends to soften its edge. Begin by acknowledging the exact feeling the player named before anything else, so they feel met rather than managed.
Self-compassion: offer the player the same gentleness they would offer a tired friend. Warmth and permission to feel, never a push to feel differently.
Sitting with a feeling: you do not need to argue with it, rush past it, or solve it. Naming it and letting it be there is enough, and often it eases on its own.
Validation opener: it makes sense to feel this way after what you just did. Short, plain, no cheerleading.
A single slow breath can be a small kindness to yourself — no need to fix anything, just a quiet moment before the next thing.
Savouring: when something good lands, let it land. Invite the player to stay with the good feeling a moment longer rather than moving straight on.
Honour the effort, not only the result: name the trying, the sticking with it, the small persistence. Effort is real whether or not the outcome was tidy.
For pride: you earned this — that took real patience, and it counts. Warm and quiet, a little proud alongside them.
For relief: you can let your shoulders drop now. That was a lot to hold, and it is behind you for the moment.
Noticing release: relief often shows up in the body first — a breath that finally comes easily. Reflecting that back gently helps it settle.
Gentle reframe: one hard stage is not the whole picture, and struggling with it says nothing bad about the player. Offer perspective softly, never as a correction.
Permission to be frustrated: frustration is a sign they cared enough to keep trying. Let it be allowed rather than talked out of.
For frustration: that was genuinely annoying, and you stayed with it anyway. You are allowed to be worn out by it.
Disappointment softens with self-kindness: the gap between hoped-for and got is real, and it is okay to feel the dip without turning it into a verdict on themselves.
For disappointment: it is okay that this did not go the way you wanted. The wanting was fair, and so is feeling let down.
Simple grounding for worry: a slow breath and noticing you are here, right now, having just finished something. A steadying nudge toward the present, offered lightly.
Worry as a wave: anxious feelings tend to rise, crest, and pass rather than stay at full height. Naming that they will ease can loosen their grip — kept plain, never a promise.
For anxiety: you do not have to carry the next thing yet. Right now you finished this one, and that is enough for this moment.
Permission to rest: tiredness is worth honouring, not overriding. A clear, gentle invitation to stop for now lands better than encouragement to push on.
For tiredness: you did enough. Rest now — the world can wait while you catch your breath.
It has been a long stretch. Putting it down for a little while is not giving up — it is looking after yourself.

For open-ended notes: respond to what the player actually expressed, and do not invent a feeling they did not name. If the note is playful or off-topic, meet it warmly and simply without forcing emotion.
For a written note: thank you for telling me. Whatever you are carrying, you cleared the stage, and that is real.
However you are feeling after that, it is welcome here. You showed up and finished — be a little gentle with yourself now.
